# Auditing and Repairing LLM-as-Judge Failures in a Production Text-to-SQL Pipeline

[All reading notes](../reading-notes.md) · [Catalog entry](../README.md#synca-audit)

**Full paper read · 2026-11-09**

[Original source](https://aclanthology.org/2026.emnlp-industry.18.pdf) · EMNLP 2026 Industry Track proceedings, pages 275-287

**Reading coverage:** All thirteen PDF pages, Sections 1-10, limitations and Appendices A-R, tables, cost assumptions, annotation details, prompts and plot captions/data. Cost and reweighting arithmetic checked against rendered PDF pages 10 and 12.

## Research question

An uncalibrated faithfulness judge can reject sound SQL by inventing constraints, corrupting acceptance and training-data decisions.

## Method

The authors audit a production judge against author-consensus labels, test prompt changes and replacement judges, and route non-unanimous ensembles to review. Independent reannotation provides a limited check on the author gold.

## Evaluation

Disagreement-enriched, random-spot-check and active-disagreement samples support different claims. Additional BIRD-financial and Spider audits examine domain shift. Agreement is Cohen's kappa, not confidence-probability calibration; routed-subset agreement is selective.

## What the results support

The weak judge over-flags many enriched cases; replacements improve agreement. The Qwen–Opus accuracy comparison remains inconclusive, and weaker ensemble members can reduce useful coverage. Strong-judge unanimity raises retained-subset agreement by abstaining.

## Limits and qualifications

One telecom deployment and small external checks limit transfer. Exact cost and population-rate headlines have unreconciled appendix arithmetic; some reported pool/exclusion counts also disagree. The taxonomy uses post-hoc grouping and LLM recoding. Deferred datasets prevent full public reproduction.

## Relevance to reliable Text-to-SQL

Provides an audit recipe and a warning against conflating selected-sample agreement, full-coverage quality and deployment safety.

## Checks against the paper

These are interpretations checked against the source, not verbatim quotations attributed to its authors.

| Opus costs about $30 per 1,000 questions from the printed token assumptions. | Appendix D gives 2,047 input and 284 output tokens at $15/$75 per million, which calculate to $52.005 per 1,000, not $30. | Appendix D Token accounting, Cloud rates and Per-1,000-question costs | Unresolved arithmetic/measurement mismatch; omit the precise 300x cost claim. |
| The reported population and pool counts are fully reconciled. | Appendix N prints 84.3+3.6+1.2≈90.6, but the sum is 89.1; Section 8 reports 1,241 after excluding 10 from 1,248, whose difference is 1,238. | Section 8; Appendix N | Do not repeat exact reweighted totals or denominators without corrected provenance. |
